About IslamicHubBuilt with sincerity,grounded in scholarshipIslamicHub began as two separate projects — ZakatCalc and Kushirik — and grew into a complete platform for learning and living the Five Pillars of Islam, with tools, education, and authentic references in one place.The teamBuilt by Muslims, for MuslimsIslamicHub is a passion project by two builders who wanted an Islamic platform that takes both technology and scholarship seriously.Zubair Idris AwedaSoftware Engineer & Technical Writer @ZubsFull-stack engineer behind the architecture, calculator engines, prayer time algorithms, and design system. Also built the original ZakatCalc and Kushirik projects that became IslamicHub.ContributionsArchitecture & routingZakat calculatorPrayer times & Qibla engineInheritance (Fara'id) engineDesign system & CSSYusuf SaifProject Manager & Technical Strategist @yusuf-saifSeasoned project manager with a robust background in technical solutions. Drives product direction, scholarly accuracy review, and ensures the platform stays true to its educational mission.ContributionsProduct strategyScholarly accuracy reviewUser experience directionContent planningDeployment & operationsOpen sourceContributions welcomeIslamicHub is open source and we actively welcome contributions — whether that's a bug fix, a new educational section, a scholarly correction, a new language, or a UI improvement.If you notice an error in a scholarly reference, a calculation that feels off, or a feature that would help the Muslim community — please open an issue or submit a pull request.View on GitHubBrowse the source code, fork the repo, and explore the project structure🐛Report an issueFound a bug, a calculation error, or an incorrect scholarly reference? Open an issue🤝How to contributeRead the contribution guide — all skill levels welcome, from code to content to translationsWays you can contribute💻Code — fix bugs, add features, improve performance📖Content — write or improve educational articles🕌Scholarship — correct or add Qur'anic / Hadith references🌍Translations — help make IslamicHub multilingual🎨Design — UI improvements, icons, accessibility🧪Testing — test across devices, browsers, and edge cases📣Sharing — spread the word to the Muslim community⭐Star on GitHub — it helps others discover the projectMissionWhy we built thisToo many Islamic tools are either too simple — stripping away nuance until they're misleading — or too academic, presenting rulings without context for ordinary Muslims. IslamicHub was built to sit in the middle: rigorous enough to trust, accessible enough for anyone.The Five Pillars are not just obligations to tick off — they are acts of worship, each with a rich scholarly tradition and deep spiritual meaning. Every page on IslamicHub tries to give you both the practice and the understanding behind it.This project began as ZakatCalc (an accurate, live-priced Zakat calculator) and Kushirik (an inheritance sharing application), two separate projects by Zubair that were merged and expanded with Yusuf's direction into what IslamicHub is today.PrinciplesWhat we stand for1Primary sources firstEvery ruling, calculation, and claim is traced back to Qur'an or authenticated Hadith. We cite the source, not just the conclusion.2All four schoolsHanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, and Hanbali positions are all considered. Consensus is stated. Differences are presented as options.3Education over efficiencyA number without understanding is not enough. Every tool section includes the scholarly basis for how the calculation works.4Privacy by designNo accounts, no personal tracking, and nothing you enter is stored on a server. Everything runs in your browser. Your financial and personal information stays with you. Anonymous usage statistics can be turned off below.5Humility before scholarshipWe are builders, not scholars. For complex situations, we always direct users to a qualified mufti or scholar.6Free, alwaysHelping Muslims fulfil their obligations should not be a commercial transaction. This platform is and will remain free.Usage statisticsHow we understand usageTo understand how IslamicHub is used and which tools are most helpful, we count anonymous usage statistics. This is strictly opt-out — you can turn it off at any time.What is counted:Page views by address (the path only, never query strings)Where a visit came from (the referring site's name only, e.g., google.com — never the full URL)Eight named actions: prayer times shown, a Zakat result reached, an inheritance result reached, an adhkar category completed, a tasbih target reached, and a round of Who am I?, a game of Kalimah or a prophets quiz finished, with no answer or scoreWhat is never sent:Any amount, weight, coordinate, place name, heir, search text, or other input you enterYour name, email, or any identifier — no cookies, no localStorage identifiers, no fingerprintingWhich specific hadith or article you read beyond the page addressStatistics are sent to GoatCounter, a cookieless, open-source analytics service. GoatCounter sees the IP address and browser type of each request (as any server does) and derives country and browser from them. It states that it never stores IP addresses and holds a scrambled form in memory for up to eight hours only to count visits.Counting happens only on the live site (islamichub.xyz) and only when configured. It is off during local development, tests, and deploy previews. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured automatically.Don't count my visitsWhen on, IslamicHub sends no usage statistics for this device.Your location:Your location is asked for only when you press a button, and is used on your device to work out prayer times and the Qibla. If you use “Use my location”, the coordinates are sent once to OpenStreetMap’s Nominatim service to find a place name. It is saved only if you choose “Remember this location” on the Prayer page, and then only on your own device, together with your calculation method and Asr method. “Forget my location” on the same page removes it. It is never sent to us, with one exception that you have to switch on yourself, described next.Notifications when the app is closed:Prayer reminders work on your device with nothing sent anywhere. If you also switch on “Also notify me when the app is closed”, a server has to send the reminder, so it keeps the least it needs to do that: the address your browser gives for sending you a notification, your location rounded to two decimal places (about 1 km), your timezone, your calculation method and Asr method, and which reminders you chose. It keeps no name, no email and no account, and it is not used for anything else. Switching that setting off, turning reminders off, or choosing “Forget my location” deletes it. If your browser stops accepting the notifications, it is deleted automatically.This is a change from our earlier “no analytics, no tracking” promise. We updated it because understanding usage helps us decide which languages to add first and which tools to improve — but we kept the core promise: your data stays on your device, and you can opt out at any time.Scholarly sourcesWhat we draw fromPrimary textsQur'an — Surah 2, 3, 4, 9, 97, 112 et al.Sahih Bukhari — Kitab al-Zakat, al-Salah, al-Sawm, al-HajjSahih Muslim — multiple booksSunan Abu Dawud · Ibn Majah · Al-TirmidhiClassical scholarshipAl-Mughni — Ibn Qudama al-MaqdisiAl-Majmu' — Imam al-NawawiBada'i' al-Sana'i' — Al-KasaniAl-Umm — Imam al-Shafi'iAl-Mudawwana — Imam MalikContemporary scholarshipFiqh al-Zakat — Sheikh Yusuf al-QaradawiContemporary Fatawa — Mufti Taqi UsmaniAAOIFI Shari'ah Standard No. 35Zakat House (Kuwait) guidelinesTechnical & data sourcesPrayer times: astronomical Adhan algorithmfawazahmed0/exchange-api — daily gold and silver prices and exchange rates (GBP/USD/EUR/SAR/NGN)Nominatim (OpenStreetMap) — reverse geocoding⚠ DisclaimerIslamicHub is an educational and guidance tool. It is not a fatwa or formal religious ruling. Prayer times are calculated astronomically and may differ from local mosque announcements. Inheritance calculations cover standard cases — complex situations require expert consultation. For personal religious rulings, consult a qualified Islamic scholar (mufti).Join us in building thisStar the repo, open an issue, or submit a pull request.
